title: A Lecture Excerpt: Gerunds and Infinitives in Academic Language

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Seitkali
dialogue.text: Today's session is about something that confuses a lot of advanced learners: when to use a gerund versus an infinitive, particularly in the pairs that change meaning. Let me start with what I consider the most important pair: "try."

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Seitkali
dialogue.text: If I say "I tried understanding the problem," I mean I made an attempt to understand it — I approached it as something to test, to experiment with. The gerund signals experiment. If I say "I tried to understand the problem," I mean I made an effort to achieve understanding, but possibly I didn't succeed. The infinitive signals effort toward a goal.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Is there a test — a quick way to remember which is which?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Seitkali
dialogue.text: The test I find most useful is the word "out." "Try + gerund" is close in meaning to "try out" — experiment, test it, see what happens. "Try + infinitive" is more like "make an effort to achieve." "Try out drinking herbal tea" (experiment) vs "try to drink herbal tea" (attempt despite difficulty).

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: What about "remember"? I always get confused about that one.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Seitkali
dialogue.text: Think of it this way: "remember + gerund" is about the past. "I remember meeting her" — the meeting is a memory. "Remember + infinitive" is about the future. "I remember to call her" — I don't forget to do something I need to do. Past event versus future task.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: And "stop" — is it the same pattern?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Seitkali
dialogue.text: "Stop" is slightly different. "Stop + gerund" means the activity ends — it stops. "She stopped working." "Stop + infinitive" expresses purpose — why you stopped. "She stopped to work" means she stopped something else in order to work. The infinitive explains the reason for stopping, not the thing that stopped.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: What about "regret"? I saw it used in a formal email yesterday — "We regret to inform you that..."

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Seitkali
dialogue.text: Ah yes — "regret to + infinitive" is used in formal contexts to introduce bad news. "I regret to inform you / to say / to announce." The regret is about the action that follows. Whereas "regret + gerund" is about something already done — you did it and now feel sorry. "I regret telling him" = I told him and now wish I hadn't.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: So in formal letters, you always use "regret + infinitive"?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Seitkali
dialogue.text: In that specific pattern, yes. "We regret to inform you..." / "I regret to say that..." It's a formula. The gerund version would imply you've already informed them and feel bad about it, which is a different situation.
